title: 1 Kings 12:16–24
context: The northern tribes reject David’s house with the cry “To your tents, Israel!” They stone Rehoboam’s labor overseer, make Jeroboam king, and leave Rehoboam with Judah and Benjamin. When Rehoboam gathers an army to restore the kingdom by force, the prophet Shemaiah tells him and the people not to fight their brothers, “for this thing is from me,” and they obey. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about judgment, the fulfillment of God’s word, and heeding the prophets.

verses.text: When all Israel saw that the king didn’t listen to them, the people answered the king, saying, “What portion have we in David? We don’t have an inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, Israel! Now see to your own house, David.” So Israel departed to their tents.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Israel sees the king will not listen, they reject David’s house: “What portion have we in David?… To your tents, Israel!” The tribes depart.

Arminian readers see the people responding to oppression with a choice of their own.
verses.reformedNotes:
The cry echoes Sheba’s rebellion in 2 Samuel 20:1. The breach is decisive.

Reformed readers see God’s word through Ahijah coming to pass. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting both the people’s grievance and the tragedy of division.

verses.text: But as for the children of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned over them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rehoboam still reigns over Israelites living in Judah’s cities. His kingdom shrinks.

Arminian readers see the limited realm left to Rehoboam as a result of his choices. What remains is far less than what he inherited.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse clarifies who remains under Rehoboam. The promise of one tribe for David’s sake is kept.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to David even in judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the fulfillment of 11:13.

verses.text: Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the men subject to forced labor; and all Israel stoned him to death with stones. King Rehoboam hurried to get himself up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rehoboam sends Adoram, the overseer of forced labor, and Israel stones him to death; Rehoboam flees to Jerusalem. The choice of envoy inflames the crisis.

Arminian readers see poor judgment compounding Rehoboam’s earlier folly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sending the labor chief was provocative. The violence shows the depth of resentment.

Reformed readers see the breach becoming irreparable. Both traditions read this plainly; Adoram may be the Adoniram of 4:6, though the text does not say.

verses.text: So Israel rebelled against David’s house to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel rebels against David’s house ‘to this day.’ The division becomes lasting.

Arminian readers see lasting consequences flowing from choices made in a single moment. A single moment of arrogance leaves a wound that lasts for generations.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘to this day’ reflects the narrator’s perspective. The schism shaped Israel’s history for centuries.

Reformed readers see God’s judgment on Solomon’s idolatry worked out over time. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the long reach of sin’s consequences.

verses.text: When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the congregation, and made him king over all Israel. There was no one who followed David’s house, except for the tribe of Judah only.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel makes Jeroboam king over all Israel; only Judah follows David’s house. Ahijah’s word is fulfilled.

Arminian readers see God’s offer to Jeroboam becoming reality through the people’s choice. The people’s decision and God’s word coincide.
verses.reformedNotes:
The northern assembly crowns Jeroboam. The kingdom is divided.

Reformed readers see God’s word accomplished through human decisions. Both traditions read this as shared ground; how Benjamin relates to ‘Judah only’ is addressed differently by interpreters, given verse 21.

verses.text: When Rehoboam had come to Jerusalem, he assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, a hundred and eighty thousand chosen men who were warriors, to fight against the house of Israel, to bring the kingdom again to Rehoboam the son of Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rehoboam assembles 180,000 warriors from Judah and Benjamin to fight Israel and restore the kingdom. He seeks to reverse the division by force.

Arminian readers see Rehoboam responding to loss with a plan for war.
verses.reformedNotes:
The large army shows Rehoboam’s determination. Benjamin stands with Judah.

Reformed readers see a king about to act against God’s purpose. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, and note that the number is reported without further detail about its composition.

verses.text: But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The word of God comes to Shemaiah, the man of God. A prophet intervenes.

Arminian readers see God speaking to prevent unnecessary bloodshed. God’s word arrives before the armies can clash.
verses.reformedNotes:
God sends his word at the decisive moment. Shemaiah is called to deliver it.

Reformed readers see God governing events through his prophetic word. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about the role of prophecy in Israel’s history and God’s care for his people.

verses.text: “Speak to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Shemaiah is to speak to Rehoboam and all Judah, Benjamin, and the rest of the people. The message is public.

Arminian readers see God addressing king and people together. No one is excluded from hearing the command.
verses.reformedNotes:
The word goes to the whole assembly, not only the king. All must hear it.

Reformed readers see God’s authority over every level of society. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, preparing for the command not to fight that follows in the next verse.

verses.text: ‘The LORD says, “You shall not go up or fight against your brothers, the children of Israel. Everyone return to his house; for this thing is from me.” ’ ” So they listened to the LORD’s word, and returned and went their way, according to the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes:
God says, “You shall not go up or fight against your brothers… for this thing is from me,” and they obey and go home. Bloodshed is averted.

Arminian readers see a king and people freely heeding God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
‘This thing is from me’ names God’s hand in the division. Obedience follows.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty and his people’s right response together. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about listening to God’s word and treating fellow Israelites as brothers.
